statement: Mia cuts a paper cube with 1 cm edges along some of its edges and lays it flat as one piece made of 6 squares. What is the perimeter of the flat shape?

choices.misconception: I pictured the six squares as a 2 by 3 block, which cannot fold into a cube, and found its perimeter of 10.
I gave the number of edges of the cube, 12, instead of the perimeter of the flat shape.
I took 1 cm off the total of 24 for each of the 5 joins, but each join hides two sides, one from each square.
I added up all the sides of the six squares, $6 \times 4 = 24$, forgetting that sides where two squares join are not on the outline.

hints: Does the answer depend on which net Mia makes?
Six squares have 24 sides in all. Count how many places two squares stay joined in a net of a cube, then remember each join hides two sides from the outline.
A net of a cube has its 6 squares joined in exactly 5 places, because a cube has 12 edges and 7 of them are cut. Each join hides 2 sides, so take $5 \times 2$ from 24.

solutions.reliable: Try the cross-shaped net: a column of four squares with one square on each side of the second square. Walking round its outline gives 14 sides of 1 cm. Every net works the same way: the six squares have $6 \times 4 = 24$ sides, and in a net the squares stay joined in exactly 5 places. Each join hides two sides, so the perimeter is $24 - 10 = 14$ cm. The transferable idea: count the sides, then subtract twice the number of joins.
solutions.elegant: Mia cuts 7 of the cube's 12 edges, since 5 must stay joined to hold 6 squares in one piece. Each cut edge becomes two pieces of outline, one on each side of the cut, so the perimeter is $7 \times 2 = 14$ cm, whatever net she makes.

whyOnTest: Nets reward thinking about how the squares join, not drawing every net; here one count of joins answers the question for all of them.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
